newsitem.title: USA: Republicans decline to write detailed budget.
newsitem.headline: Republicans decline to write detailed budget.

text.p: Republican leaders in Congress declined Tuesday to give President Clinton ironclad guarantees they would support his tax cuts or domestic programmes as part of an agreement to balance the budget.

With the budget deal only loosely sewn together, the White House and Democratic lawmakers pressed resistant Republicans to add details to the budget before it is presented to Congress this month. But Republicans said the pressure would not work.
"They are continuing to want to spend more and we continue to want to restrain spending. That is the crux of the battle," Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott told reporters.

Lott accused the Clinton administration of pushing too far on some tax issues. "Both sides are trying to ... clear up misunderstandings and I think that the administration is trying to push the envelope beyond what was agreed to by any stretch of the imagination," the Mississippi Republican said.
"We agreed to no limits on capital gains or estate tax, and we're not getting into that," he said.

To much fanfare on May 2, Republican congressional leaders and Clinton announced in separate news conferences that they had reached an agreement to balance the budget by 2002, cut taxes by a net $85 billion over five years, trim Medicare health care spending and give the president money for many of his domestic programmes.
But there was no ink to dry on the pact. No joint statement was issued and all sides have spent much of time since then trying to nail down exactly the details of their agreement.

Lott and House Speaker Newt Gingrich were to draft a letter stating that their goals were to give Clinton education tax credits he sought, among other items. But Lott stated that the letter would not bind Congress during the months of budget negotiations ahead.

Without the sought-after guarantees, the top Democrat on the House Budget Committee, Representative John Spratt of South Carolina, might offer a Democratic alternative budget rather than back the budget deal, a Democratic source said.
The panel was scheduled to begin open, public debate on the budget Wednesday. The Senate Budget Committeee, meanwhile, did not expect to consider its version until Thursday at the earliest.
Budget leaders of both parties met privately Tuesday with administration officials in an attempt to work out differences before the public meetings.

But the Clinton administration will not have the guarantees it sought on specific tax cuts to benefit education and children, nor will the budget direct other committees to approve levels of spending for the president's priorities, House Majority Leader Dick Armey said.
